newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Economics of Information gurus win Nobel prize. [CORRECTED 13:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Economics of Information gurus win Nobel prize. [CORRECTED 13:45 GMT]

text.p: Two financial gurus whose work set the 20th Century agenda for matching social responsiblity with incentives and whose work has been crucial for global tax policies were awarded the 1996 Nobel Economic Prize on Tuesday.

British professor James Mirrlees, 60 (corrects age from "50"), of Cambridge University and 82-year-old Canadian William Vickrey won the prize for their fundamental contribution to "the economic theory of incentives under asymmetric information."
Assymetric information occurs when decision makers have different information but have to make decisions based on that information.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which awards the prize on behalf of the country's Central Bank, the Riksbank, said Mirrlees' and Vickrey's work centred on one of the liveliest areas of economic research.
The two men zeroed in on how governments, companies or any organisation could cope with constantly lacking complete information but having to make strategic decisions.

"For example a bank does not have the complete information about lenders' future income; the owners of a firm may not have the same detailed information about costs and competitive conditions as the managing director," the academy said.

Research on the "economics of information" had generated a better understanding of insurance markets, credit markets, auctions, the internal organisation of firms, wage forms, tax systems, social insurance, competitive conditions, political institutions etc," it added.

Vickrey was born in Victoria, British Columbia, Canada, in 1914 and attended Yale, graduating in 1935. He is now Professor Emeritus at Columbia University, New York, where he also served as a tax advisor between 1937 and 1947.
Mirrlees was born in Minnigaff, Scotland in 1936 and is now teaching economics at the University of Cambridge, in England. He worked at Oxford University from 1969 to 1995.
The two men will share the prize, worth $1.12 million.

Vickrey originally became known for his work on income taxation, rewriting the 19th Century philosophy that all differences in income should be neutralised by taxation, implying strongly progressive tax rates.
Vickrey in the 1940s said progressive taxation affected individuals' incentive to work and he reformulated the problem so that individuals' productivity should not be penalised by tax schedules.
Some 25 years later Mirrlees mastered the mathematical complications of Vickrey's work, drastically simplifying the issue and applying it to many other areas of economic theory.
"It has therefore had a large bearing on the treatment of many issues of economic theory," the academy added.

The two mens' work has had a major bearing on the financing of public services. Vickrey carried out a study of the New York subway fare system in the 1950s that make him stand out for most economists, who stick to theory rather than practice, the academy added.
